claims.text: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi or its high-entropy-alloy derivatives have coercive fields of 100 Oe or lower.
Controlled low-temperature annealing can induce nanoscale secondary-phase precipitation in an fcc FeCoNi-based matrix.
The annealing-induced precipitates can remain uniformly dispersed and nanoscale while preserving the fcc matrix.
The resulting nanoscale precipitates act as domain-wall pinning centers.
Pinning by the precipitates hinders domain-wall motion and raises the energy barrier for domain-wall movement.
The increased barrier to domain-wall motion enhances coercivity.
The annealing treatment will increase the coercive field beyond 100 Oe relative to the unannealed baseline.
The annealing treatment will have minimal impact on saturation magnetization.
The proposed effect is conditional on the precipitates remaining nanoscale and uniformly distributed.
Significant phase separation or excessive precipitate coarsening may invalidate the coercivity enhancement.
The magnitude of coercivity improvement depends on annealing conditions and precipitate characteristics.
Room-temperature hysteresis measurements by VSM or SQUID can determine the coercive field of treated and control samples.
TEM or SEM can be used to assess the presence and distribution of nanoscale precipitates.
Failure to obtain a coercivity increase exceeding 50% over the control is specified as a falsifying outcome.
Failure to confirm uniformly dispersed nanoscale precipitates is specified as a falsifying outcome.

contradictions.description: The prediction requires coercivity to exceed 100 Oe, whereas the falsification rule requires an increase exceeding 50% over the control. These thresholds are not equivalent: an outcome can exceed 100 Oe but fail the 50% criterion, or exceed 50% while remaining below 100 Oe.
